In mathematics, the '''Wirtinger inequality''', named after [[Wilhelm Wirtinger]], is a fundamental result in [[linear algebra|complex linear algebra]] which relates the symplectic and volume forms of a [[hermitian inner product]]. It has important consequences in [[complex geometry]], such as showing that the normalized [[exterior power]]s of the [[Kähler manifold|Kähler form]] of a [[Kähler manifold]] are [[calibrated geometry|calibrations]].

==Statement==
Consider a [[real vector space]] with positive-definite [[inner product]] {{math|''g''}}, symplectic form {{math|''&omega;''}}, and almost-complex structure {{math|''J''}}, linked by {{math|''&omega;''(''u'', ''v'') {{=}} ''g''(''J''(''u''), ''v'')}} for any vectors {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}}. Then for any orthonormal vectors {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} there is
:<math> (\underbrace{\omega\wedge\cdots\wedge\omega}_{k\text{ times}})(v_1,\ldots,v_{2k}) \leq k !.</math>
There is equality if and only if the span of {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} is closed under the operation of {{math|''J''}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Federer|1y=1969|1loc=Section 1.8.2}}

In the language of the [[current (mathematics)|comass]] of a form, the Wirtinger theorem (although without precision about when equality is achieved) can also be phrased as saying that the comass of the form {{math|''&omega;'' ∧ ⋅⋅⋅ ∧ ''&omega;''}} is equal to {{math|''k''!}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Federer|1y=1969|1loc=Section 1.8.2}}

==Proof==
==={{math|''k'' {{=}} 1}}===
In the special case {{math|''k'' {{=}} 1}}, the Wirtinger inequality is a special case of the [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality]]:
:<math>\omega(v_1,v_2)=g(J(v_1),v_2)\leq \|J(v_1)\|_g\|v_2\|_g=1.</math>
According to the equality case of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, equality occurs if and only if {{math|''J''(''v''<sub>1</sub>)}} and {{math|''v''<sub>2</sub>}} are collinear, which is equivalent to the span of {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub>, ''v''<sub>2</sub>}} being closed under {{mvar|J}}.
==={{math|''k'' > 1}}===
Let {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} be fixed, and let {{mvar|T}} denote their span. Then there is an orthonormal basis {{math|''e''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''e''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} of {{mvar|T}} with dual basis {{math|''w''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''w''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} such that
:<math>\iota^\ast\omega=\sum_{j=1}^k\omega(e_{2j-1},e_{2j})w_{2j-1}\wedge w_{2j},</math>
where {{math|''&iota;''}} denotes the inclusion map from {{mvar|T}} into {{mvar|V}}.{{sfnm|1a1=McDuff|1a2=Salamon|1y=2017|1loc=Lemma 2.4.5}} This implies
:<math>\underbrace{\iota^\ast\omega\wedge\cdots\wedge \iota^\ast\omega}_{k\text{ times}}=k!\prod_{i=1}^k\omega(e_{2i-1},e_{2i})w_1\wedge \cdots\wedge w_{2k},</math>
which in turn implies
:<math>(\underbrace{\omega\wedge\cdots\wedge\omega}_{k\text{ times}})(e_1,\ldots,e_{2k})=k!\prod_{i=1}^k\omega(e_{2i-1},e_{2i})\leq k!,</math>
where the inequality follows from the previously-established {{math|''k'' {{=}} 1}} case. If equality holds, then according to the {{math|''k'' {{=}} 1}} equality case, it must be the case that {{math|''&omega;''(''e''<sub>2''i'' − 1</sub>, ''e''<sub>2''i''</sub>) {{=}} ±1}} for each {{mvar|i}}. This is equivalent to either {{math|''&omega;''(''e''<sub>2''i'' − 1</sub>, ''e''<sub>2''i''</sub>) {{=}} 1}} or {{math|''&omega;''(''e''<sub>2''i''</sub>, ''e''<sub>2''i'' − 1</sub>) {{=}} 1}}, which in either case (from the {{math|''k'' {{=}} 1 }} case) implies that the span of {{math|''e''<sub>2''i'' − 1</sub>, ''e''<sub>2''i''</sub>}} is closed under {{math|''J''}}, and hence that the span of {{math|''e''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''e''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} is closed under {{mvar|J}}.

Finally, the dependence of the quantity
:<math>(\underbrace{\omega\wedge\cdots\wedge\omega}_{k\text{ times}})(v_1,\ldots,v_{2k})</math>
on {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} is only on the quantity {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub> ∧ ⋅⋅⋅ ∧ ''v''<sub>2''k''</sub>}}, and from the orthonormality condition on {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>2''k''</sub>}}, this wedge product is well-determined up to a sign. This relates the above work with {{math|''e''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''e''<sub>2''k''</sub>}} to the desired statement in terms of {{math|''v''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>2''k''</sub>}}.

==Consequences==
Given a [[complex manifold]] with [[hermitian metric]], the Wirtinger theorem immediately implies that for any {{math|2''k''}}-dimensional [[embedded submanifold]] {{mvar|M}}, there is
:<math>\operatorname{vol}(M)\geq\frac{1}{k!}\int_M \omega^k,</math>
where {{math|''&omega;''}} is the [[Kähler form]] of the metric. Furthermore, equality is achieved if and only if {{mvar|M}} is a [[complex submanifold]].{{sfnm|1a1=Griffiths|1a2=Harris|1y=1978|1loc=Section 0.2}} In the special case that the hermitian metric satisfies the [[Kähler metric|Kähler condition]], this says that {{math|{{sfrac|1|''k''!}}''&omega;''<sup>''k''</sup>}} is a [[calibrated geometry|calibration]] for the underlying Riemannian metric, and that the corresponding [[calibrated geometry|calibrated submanifolds]] are the complex submanifolds of complex dimension {{mvar|k}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Harvey|1a2=Lawson|1y=1982}} This says in particular that every complex submanifold of a Kähler manifold is a [[minimal submanifold]], and is even volume-minimizing among all submanifolds in its [[homology class]].

Using the Wirtinger inequality, these facts even extend to the more sophisticated context of [[current (mathematics)|currents]] in Kähler manifolds.{{sfnm|1a1=Federer|1y=1969|1loc=Section 5.4.19}}
